article.headline: A Power Inventor's Long Game in the AI Infrastructure Buildout
article.lede: A detailed investment post by @joedab12 makes the case for Vicor Corporation (VICR) as a structural beneficiary of the AI infrastructure boom — not through chip design or software, but through the unglamorous physics of delivering tens of thousands of amperes to a hungry processor. The argument rests on three pillars: a manufacturing ramp linked to the wafer-scale AI accelerator market, an accelerating patent-royalty stream from International Trade Commission victories, and a speculative but technically coherent potential design-in on NVIDIA's next-generation GPU architecture. The poster frames it as a repeat of a prior successful call on Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI), which he claims to have recommended in the $50s before a roughly 300-percent gain.
article.body:
The engineering premise is simple to state and hard to commercialise. As AI accelerators push core voltages below 0.85 volts and current demands past tens of thousands of amperes at the die edge, the conventional approach — routing power laterally across a printed circuit board through a *power-distribution network* (PDN) before it descends to the chip — wastes unacceptable fractions of energy to resistance and inductance. Vicor Corporation (VICR) has spent most of a decade building its answer: *vertical power delivery* (VPD), in which a thin current-multiplier module called a *VTM* mounts directly beneath the processor on the underside of the board and pushes current straight up into the chip face. Second-generation VPD, disclosed on Vicor's Q1 2026 earnings call, achieves 3 amperes per square millimetre at a current multiplication factor of up to 40 times inside a 1.5mm package — parameters targeted at 3nm and 5nm process nodes.

The company that Vicor (VICR) is almost certainly supplying is **Cerebras Systems**, maker of the *Wafer-Scale Engine* (WSE) — a single silicon die roughly the size of a dinner plate, drawing approximately 23 kilowatts per system. At that scale, vertical delivery is not a preference but a necessity; routing power laterally to the edge of a wafer that large would exhaust any practical conductor. Management has described its lead customer in recent earnings calls as "the maker of a wafer-scale-engine-based AI accelerator," while in the same Q1 2026 call citing Cerebras by name as the archetype of the power-density problem VPD is designed to solve. Neither company has issued a press release confirming the relationship; semiconductor analysts who have traced the supply chain independently treat it as established fact. Cerebras does not appear to be publicly traded, making Vicor the most direct listed proxy for this exposure.

The manufacturing story is real but the timeline is overstated. Vicor (VICR) operates a proprietary *3Di* fabrication process — a form of three-dimensional chip stacking — at its Federal Street fab in Andover, Massachusetts, which the company owns outright. Management has confirmed a long-run annual revenue capacity target of $1.5 billion for the facility, with a second 3Di production line to be installed in the second half of 2026. However, 2026 full-year revenue guidance stands at roughly $570 million, and management on the Q1 2026 earnings call explicitly declined to commit to a year-end 2026 target for the $1.5 billion ceiling, calling such specificity "unwise." What is confirmed: a $301 million backlog as of Q1 2026, up 70% sequentially, and a self-description as "essentially sold out for the foreseeable future." An unnamed major *hyperscaler* is reported to have tested second-generation VPD, with results satisfactory enough to motivate additional capacity commitments at Andover.

A parallel revenue stream from intellectual property may prove as durable as the product business. In February 2025 the *International Trade Commission* (ITC) upheld Vicor's (VICR) power-converter patents in Case 337-TA-1370, issuing a Limited Exclusion Order that bars the importation of infringing modules and computing systems. Delta Electronics (2308.TW) and Quanta Computer (2382.TW) are among the named respondents. Vicor expects nearly $300 million in cumulative settlement and licensing revenues through 2026 from that case. Royalties grew from $2.8 million in 2022 to $57.4 million across full-year 2025 — a compelling trajectory, though the tweet's "$90 million annual run-rate" claim is not supported by any public filing or earnings guidance. A second ITC investigation (337-TA-1484), filed in early 2026, names **Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR)** and Delta as respondents — a striking escalation, given that MPWR displaced Vicor at NVIDIA (NVDA) during the H100 generation and now commands roughly 6.7 times Vicor's market capitalisation on approximately 6 times the revenue.

The thesis closes with its most speculative proposition. "Feynman" is a confirmed NVIDIA (NVDA) GPU architecture announced at GTC 2025, planned for 2028 on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's (TSM) 1.6-nanometre A16 node. At that process node, with three-dimensional die stacking, power density requirements will likely surpass what conventional lateral delivery can sustain — making vertical delivery a logical beneficiary. But no public statement from either company confirms a Vicor (VICR) design engagement, and 2028 is a long way from a confirmed customer win. Undergirding the entire argument is founder Patrizio Vinciarelli, who at 79 holds 27.1% of Vicor's publicly traded common stock and 94.1% of the super-voting Class B shares, translating to 79.1% of total voting power — a degree of founder control essentially without parallel among profitable, publicly traded American semiconductor firms, and a structural shield against the activist pressure that could derail a multi-year manufacturing ramp.

concepts.definition: Vicor's patented power architecture in which a current-multiplier module mounts directly beneath a processor on the underside of a circuit board and delivers current vertically into the chip face, rather than routing it laterally across the board. This eliminates the resistive and inductive losses of conventional power distribution and becomes critical as chip voltages fall below 1 volt and current demands climb into the tens of thousands of amperes per die.

The network of conductors — copper planes, traces, decoupling capacitors, and voltage regulators — on a circuit board that routes power from a supply to a processor. As chip voltages shrink and current demands grow with each semiconductor generation, the PDN's parasitic resistance and inductance increasingly limit how much power can be delivered efficiently; this is the fundamental constraint Vicor's VPD architecture is designed to overcome.

Vicor's current-multiplier chip that converts an intermediate bus voltage — typically 48 volts — to the sub-1-volt level a processor requires, while multiplying the delivered current by up to 40 times. In the VPD architecture the VTM is packaged in a 1.5mm-thick module and mounts on the underside of a circuit board directly beneath the processor die, minimising the distance current must travel after voltage transformation.

An AI processor built from an entire silicon wafer rather than individual chips diced from it. By eliminating inter-chip boundaries, a WSE removes communication bottlenecks but generates extraordinary power density in the process. Cerebras Systems' CS-3 system draws approximately 23 kilowatts per unit — creating the exact current-delivery challenge Vicor's VPD architecture is engineered to solve.

Vicor's proprietary three-dimensional chip-stacking and packaging process used to manufacture its power modules. Rather than assembling components on a flat substrate, 3Di stacks power-conversion elements vertically, enabling the high current density and thin form factor that vertical power delivery requires. Vicor operates its 3Di process at its Andover, Massachusetts fab, which the company owns outright — an unusual degree of vertical integration for a semiconductor firm of its size.

An order issued by the U.S. International Trade Commission prohibiting the importation of products found to infringe a domestic patent holder's rights. Unlike a federal court injunction, a LEO operates at the border and does not require a showing of irreparable harm, making it a potent enforcement tool for patent holders whose competitors manufacture abroad and import into the United States.

A company that operates cloud computing infrastructure at the largest scale — Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta among the canonical examples. In semiconductor analysis the term doubles as shorthand for the dominant buyers of AI chips and power systems, whose capital expenditure decisions effectively set the volume and trajectory of the entire supply chain.

Under Nasdaq rules, a company qualifies as a controlled company when a single shareholder or group controls more than 50% of total voting power. Controlled companies are exempt from certain board independence requirements. At Vicor, founder Patrizio Vinciarelli controls 79.1% of voting power through Class B super-voting shares (which carry 10 votes each), qualifying it for the designation and giving him effective veto power over all major corporate decisions.

article.fact_check: Three claims in the post require qualification. First, 'max capacity by year-end' overstates Vicor's own guidance: the $1.5 billion capacity target for Fab One is real, but management explicitly declined on the Q1 2026 earnings call to commit to a year-end 2026 timeline, calling such specificity unwise; full-year 2026 revenue guidance is approximately $570 million. Second, the '$90 million annual royalty revenue' figure has not been achieved or guided publicly — full-year 2025 royalties totalled $57.4 million, up from $46.6 million in 2024. Third, the claim that Monolithic Power Systems has '13x the market cap' of Vicor is materially overstated; as of May 2026, MPWR trades at approximately 6.7 times Vicor's market capitalisation on roughly 6 times the revenue.

ticker_vicr.name: Vicor Corporation
ticker_vicr.blurb: Vicor Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, and markets modular power components and power systems for converting electrical power in electrically powered devices. The company offers a range of brick-format DC-DC converters, complementary components for AC line rectification and filtering, and input/output voltage products. Vicor serves customers in the United States, Europe, Asia Pacific, and internationally, and is known for its high-performance power management solutions.
ticker_vicr.recent: As of May 6, 2026, Vicor's stock closed at $280.34, up 5.39% on the day, with a 52-week range of $39.64 to $293.95. The company reported strong financials with revenue of $426.70M (up 15.6% year-over-year) and net income of $136.68M (up 490.6%). Analysts have a Strong Buy rating with a price target of $217.50, though the stock trades above that level.

ticker_mpwr.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
ticker_mpwr.blurb: A fab-light analog company that designs high-density power-management integrated circuits — the chips that step a server's intermediate-bus voltage down to the sub-1-volt rail an AI accelerator actually consumes. MPWR moved from a broad-based analog supplier into the dominant provider of GPU-adjacent power modules during the H100 generation, displacing the incumbent Vicor at Nvidia. Its modules are characterised by very high current density and tight integration, which matter enormously as AI racks push past 100 kilowatts.
ticker_mpwr.recent: In early 2026, management raised the floor on its enterprise-data growth target to 50-percent-plus from a prior 30-to-40 percent range, citing acceleration in Nvidia Blackwell shipments. Analyst notes suggest MPWR may take roughly 70 percent of power-management sockets on the forthcoming Vera Rubin GPU platform (VR200 NVL144 and R200 HGX), potentially adding more than $100 million to 2026 estimates. The stock has gained roughly 90 percent over the trailing twelve months and trades near all-time highs, leaving the AI exposure largely in the price.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_2308-tw.name: Delta Electronics, Inc.
ticker_2308-tw.blurb: Delta Electronics, Inc. is a global provider of power and thermal management solutions, serving industries such as data centers, renewable energy, electric vehicles, and industrial automation. Headquartered in Taiwan, the company operates in Mainland China, the United States, Thailand, and other international markets. With a market capitalization of approximately NT$5.7 trillion, Delta is a leading player in the power electronics sector, known for its high-efficiency products and strong focus on innovation.
ticker_2308-tw.recent: In the past 30 days, Delta Electronics' stock has shown volatility but remains supported by long-term secular trends in electric vehicles, renewables, and data centers. Analysts have lifted price targets, citing AI innovations driving stronger growth outlook, with earnings forecast to grow 28.11% per year. The stock is currently trading at a 2.6% discount to its estimated fair value, according to Simply Wall St.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.
